source.title: Better audio representations are more brain-like: linking model-brain alignment with performance in downstream auditory tasks
source.authors: Leonardo Pepino; P. Riera; J. Kamienkowski; Luciana Ferrer

record.tranche_reason: The study discusses the Platonic Representation Hypothesis, but measures audio-model-to-human-fMRI alignment rather than similarity between independently trained models or any other behavior named by the claim versions.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own measurements of audio-model alignment with human brain activity and its relation to downstream performance. Those are related findings, but the measured comparison is between a model and fMRI responses, not between independently trained models. It also does not test vision-language alignment on paired data, seed convergence, representation interchangeability, or recurring features. Numerical values shown only in figures are not transcribed here; rows below include results the text describes explicitly.
record.test_reason: All results compare audio-model representations with human auditory-cortex fMRI (voxel regression, RSA). None compare independently trained models with each other. The authors present the brain as 'another top-performing model' and claim support for the Platonic Representation Hypothesis. Still, model-to-brain alignment is a related but different construct from the convergence the versions name, so it is recorded under fits_no_version, not as a test of V1 or V2.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that better downstream audio performance goes with stronger auditory-cortex alignment (r>0.8). They find that brain alignment emerges early in EnCodecMAE pretraining without being optimized, and that diverse pretraining data helps. They frame this as support for the Platonic Representation Hypothesis, treating the brain as another high-performing model. They note that high-performing models with low brain similarity would count against the hypothesis, and that results may depend on the 165-stimulus set and the six tasks.
record.recipe_differences: The paper measures model-to-brain alignment using voxel-wise and component-wise regression and RSA, rather than measuring similarity between independently trained models using the Platonic Representation Hypothesis methods. It does not apply the original method.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports that alignment differs with pretraining data and auditory region/layer. It notes that regression and RSA give consistent overall conclusions but differ in how pronounced model differences are. The authors also caution that results may depend on the 165-stimulus set, the six selected downstream tasks, and downstream-model design.

fits_no_version.finding: Overall HEAREval downstream performance correlates with voxel-regression brain alignment: r=0.90 (NH2015) and 0.89 (B2021). With four weak models excluded, r=0.71 and 0.70. RSA gives consistent results.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Audio models that perform better on diverse auditory tasks align more with human auditory-cortex fMRI responses.

fits_no_version.finding: EnCodecMAE's RSA similarity to auditory-cortex fMRI rises during self-supervised pretraining. The rise has region- and layer-specific exceptions.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Model-to-brain alignment emerges during self-supervised pretraining without a brain objective.

fits_no_version.finding: ECMAE variants trained on diverse audio align with fMRI better than the speech-only LibriLight variant, under both regression and RSA. The authors note the stimulus set may favour diverse-sound models.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Pretraining-data diversity affects audio-model-to-brain alignment for naturalistic sound stimuli.

fits_no_version.finding: Model size variants (ECMAE S/B/L; Dasheng B/XL/XXL) are included, but the text reports no size-alignment trend. In Fig. 2 the larger variants do not rank above the base models. Finetuning and iterative target refinement show no significant change in alignment.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Within a model family, larger size does not clearly increase model-to-brain alignment for auditory fMRI.

record.problems: The authors note that fMRI has low temporal resolution; the dataset includes only 165 auditory stimuli and may favor models trained on diverse sounds; the set of six downstream tasks does not fully represent auditory abilities; the model-performance range is unevenly covered; and downstream rankings may depend on task and downstream-model design. Model-level scores in the main figures are not provided numerically in the text.
record.rows_left_out: No rows were omitted under the 60-row limit. The paper also reports individual-model scores and component-wise results in Figures 2, 4 and S1 and task/component correlations in Table 1; these are not cataloged as claim-version results because they measure audio-model-to-brain alignment, not convergence between independently trained models.

untested.parts: No model-to-model similarity is measured, and no test of whether it rises with scale or capability.
No paired image-caption comparison between vision and language models.
No stitching, cross-model mapping or relative-representation tests.
No analysis of features or circuits recurring across models.
Regression and RSA are compared only for model-to-brain alignment, not for model-to-model convergence.
No measure of the plateau or causes of inter-model alignment.

record.verdict_notes: The record's relation (discusses) and tranche (T6) are kept. The paper's PRH framing rests on model-brain rather than model-model alignment, so no version verdicts are given. Size variants exist but no size-alignment analysis is reported.

versions.untested_parts: The paper does not measure similarity between independently trained models, or whether that similarity rises with model size and capability.
No comparison across random initializations of the same architecture or analysis of shared features or subspaces.
No mapping, stitching, relative-representation, or unpaired interchangeability test.
No analysis of recurring interpretable features or circuits across models.
The paper compares two measures of model-to-brain alignment and varies auditory stimuli/pretraining data, but does not test metric or input dependence of convergence between models.
The paper does not measure whether inter-model alignment plateaus or whether shared training data or objectives explain such alignment.
